newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia sorghum rises dramatically - Grainco.
newsitem.headline: Australia sorghum rises dramatically - Grainco.

text.p: In a dramatic week in Australia's domestic sorghum market, values in south Queensland continued to rise on concern about lack of rainfall and the progress of the winter crop, Grainco Ltd said in its weekly market report.

Rob Brealey, trading manager of the Queensland grain co-operative, said central Queensland values continued to trade above export levels as strong demand from both southern Queensland and Victoria drove the market in the short-term.
That could turn around quickly if the futures market were to move higher on U.S. weather/crop concerns or if significant rain fell in Australia's southern market, he said.
Sorghum finished the week in south Queensland at around A$145-A$150 a tonne on-farm, reflecting dry weather pressure on the market, he said.
Short-term domestic gains appeared to be driven by consumers and trade participants who found themselves short for July-August requirements, he said.

Central Queensland values continued to reflect an A$8 to A$10 a tonne premium over current export values, reflecting the sizeable gains southern domestic markets had made over the past two to three weeks, he said.
Growers needed to watch both the domestic and international markets over the next couple of weeks for longer-term price direction, he said.
Weather concerns in North America and the Eureopean Union (EU) had marginally lifted support levels for barley, he said.
Dryness in some areas of the U.S. corn belt was supporting feed values, while parts of the EU were experiencing the worst floods in history, he said.

Last week, Australian new crop feed barley was offered at around US$135 a tonne free on board (fob). This week buyers were expected at that level while sellers were expected to wait for a better view of weather impact on production.
With malt barley values nominally around US$165-$170 a tonne fob, neither buyers or sellers seemed prepared to move while the EU and Australian situations remained in question.
Australia's impact on world markets should not be under-estimated as the country was the largest exporter of malting barley to the giant Chinese market, he said.
Domestic old crop feed barley prices finished the week at around A$185-A$190 a tonne delivered Brisbane for August, a significant premium over current export values.

New crop values finished the week at A$170 a tonne delivered Brisbane for November-December and A$175 a tonne for October delivery, in line with generally stronger feed grain values because of dry weather and struggling winter crops.
New crop domestic malting barley values were beginning to move away from export values as the liklihood of a domestic shortage became a real possibility, he said.
Prices finished the week at A$195 a tonne delivered Brisbane, up A$10 on the week.
Trading in cottonseed kept up the pace of recent weeks with activity in both the export and domestic markets.
While much of the heat had left the U.S. market recently, Korean and Japanese cottonseed consumers were believed to still have a considerable volume of seed to cover, he said.

Despite the continued tightening of Australian supply and demand, many Asian consumers still felt seed was freely available. Some bids were being received at up to US$20 a tonne below current market leverls, he said.
Australian offering prices ranged between US$220 a tonne and $230 a tonne delivered Japanese port for August to September, with stronger prices being quoted for the first quarter of 1998.
This reflected ex-gin Downs prices of A$160-A$165. Domestic business was becoming slightly stronger under the influence of ongoing dry weather, trading at A$165-A$170 ex Downs gin basis, he said.
Seed prices in northern NSW and central Queensland also firmed on dry conditions, trading between A$155-A$165 a tonne.
The price outlook remains firm with stocks tight and dry weather set to continue, Brealey said.

The pulses market turned around slightly last week with container traders attempting to snap up any remaining tonnage in old crop chickpeas along the eastern seabord. Old crop chickpeas traded up to A$370 a tonne delivered port on small quantities.
With most of the old crop chickpeas already shipped to India, sentiment from the sub-continent seems to suggest an improvement in prices as the new crop approaches.
The combination of a domestic surplus of sunflower seed and weaker oilseeds markets dragged domestic oilseed prices down over the week.
Prices fell by A$10 a tonne and it appeared that central Queensland may produce 10,000-15,000 tonnes in excess of domestic requirements, Brealey said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
